sentences: Thousands of small dots fill the canvas, and above them rises one great triangle.
This is Ad Parnassum, painted in 1932 by Paul Klee.
At first it looks like a mosaic, or like light trembling on water.
Only slowly does a mountain begin to appear.
The title refers to Mount Parnassus, the home of Apollo and the Muses in Greek myth.
Ad Parnassum means toward Parnassus.
For centuries, climbing that mountain stood for striving toward the highest peak of art, and Klee knowingly borrowed that old image.
Klee was born near Bern in Switzerland and worked for many years in Germany.
When he painted this picture, he was teaching at the art academy in Düsseldorf.
His notebooks and teaching were full of ideas about line, colour and rhythm.
In 1931 and 1932, he became absorbed in pictures built up from small dots, a kind of pointillism of his own.
Ad Parnassum is regarded as the crowning work of that period.
The Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern once devoted an entire exhibition to this single canvas.
Now look toward the top of the canvas.
Bold lines form a huge triangle.
It could be a roof, a mountain or a pyramid.
Klee lets all three readings live side by side.
A few years earlier he had travelled to Egypt, and that journey is often linked to this painting.
Near it floats a round orange disc.
It reads like a sun, or like light spreading from behind the mountain.
Against the cooler field of dots, it glows warmly, like the point the whole picture turns around.
Look lower down as well.
There is a shape that opens like a gate, perhaps the way into the mountain.
Besides Egypt, the outline of the Niesen, a pointed mountain beside Lake Thun in Switzerland, is said to have inspired the picture.
Now come close and look at the dots one by one.
Klee first laid down squares of casein paint directly on unprimed canvas.
Over them he stamped small white dots, then glazed them with oil paint thinned with turpentine.
Each dot was placed by hand.
That is why the dots look alike yet are all slightly different.
Together, those tiny differences make the whole surface shimmer like light.
Many viewers feel a musical rhythm in it, as if the colours were notes repeating and changing.
The following year, after the Nazis came to power, Klee left Germany and returned to Bern.
He died in 1940.
Since 1935 this painting has been on long-term loan to the Kunstmuseum Bern from the museum's friends' association.
Step back again and watch the dots gather into a single mountain.
Then ask yourself what your own Parnassus might be, the peak you would most like to climb.
